query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the high-temperature BCC phase becomes thermodynamically unstable below approximately 600 °C due to strong Al–Ni and Al–Co pair interactions that drive spinodal decomposition and promote B2 ordering.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 synthesized in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state by rapid quenching from above the ordering temperature.
generation.intervention: Isothermal annealing at temperatures between 550 °C and 600 °C with controlled cooling rates.
generation.conditions: Annealing performed in an inert atmosphere for durations between 1–10 hours, with precise temperature control (±1 °C) and uniform sample geometry to minimize thermal gradients.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of ordered B2 domains within the BCC matrix, accompanied by compositional modulations driven by Al–Ni/Co interactions.
generation.mechanism: Strong preferential pair interactions lower the free energy for an ordered B2 arrangement. Below ~600 °C, the disordered BCC phase undergoes spinodal-like decomposition as atomic mobility decreases, enabling ordering despite competing kinetic barriers.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will show the emergence of superlattice reflections (indicative of B2 ordering) in X-ray/neutron diffraction, sharp exothermic peaks in DSC corresponding to the ordering transition, and TEM images revealing increased ordered domain volume (an increase by over 50% relative to the quenched baseline).
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 retaining a metastable, single-phase high-temperature BCC structure.
generation.boundary: The transformation is expected only below approximately 600 °C; if the sample is held at or above 600 °C or cooled too rapidly, the ordered phase will not form.
generation.uncertainty: Exact ordering kinetics may be sensitive to slight compositional fluctuations and nonuniform thermal gradients; however, strict process control is expected to reduce these uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples: one set is rapidly quenched to retain the high-temperature BCC state and the other is annealed at 550–600 °C for varying durations. Characterize all samples using XRD, DSC, and TEM.
measurements: XRD for detection of B2 superlattice peaks
DSC to identify exothermic peaks associated with ordering
TEM (with EDS mapping) to observe nanoscale compositional modulations and ordered domains
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant evidence of B2 ordering versus the quenched baseline, or if ordering signatures appear markedly above 600 °C, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this report, we establish a force-field for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy and validate it by comparing structural properties, relative stability, and pair probabilities with first-principles calculations and limited experimental results. After the validation, we employ the new potential to investigate the large-scale deformation characteristics of Al0.1CrCoFeNi using atomistic MD simulations. Thus, we address the absence of well-developed force-field functions for high-entropy alloys and provide the EAM-LJ parameters to define the self- and cross-interactions of the participating elements in the alloy. In Al0.1CrCoFeNi, the electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations predict clustering driven by Al-Ni pair correlations (forcing Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering behavior). The MD simulations are in agreement with the clustering trend, as given by the large clustering domains of like pairs dominated by Al-Al. Although an increase in temperature reduces the clustering strength of like pairs, Al-Al correlations still dominate. cited_evidence.text: We observe the following trends for AlxCoCrFeNi, for the range 1 < x < 2, summarized in Fig. 7: there is a strongly x-dependent B2-ordering temperature, ranging in the simulations from approximately 1220 °C for x = 1 to 1850 °C for x = 2. For x = 1, this value is close to the temperature where B2 superlattice peaks are first observed (Fig. 4b). These compounds melt near 1300 °C (Fig. 4a, b). Thus, for x = 2, the prediction is that the compound will have strong B2 order on solidification, consistent with our scattering experiments (Fig. 4a). We predict that the system will have weak B2 order on solidification for most compositions in this range. We further predict a weakly x-dependent temperature where the B2 and BCC solid solutions become strongly separated. This unexpectedly sharp transformation occurs very closely to an observed change in the microstructure, using in situ microscopy during heating (Fig. 6b, c), and at a temperature very close to a peak observed through calorimetry for x = 1 (Supplementary Figure S3). papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlxCoCrFeNi alloys (with compositions in the range 1 < x < 2, representative of Al-containing HEAs)
papers.approach: Combined high-throughput Monte Carlo simulations with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, and experimental techniques (neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry) to map temperature‐dependent ordering and phase evolution.
papers.findings: Identified a two‐step transformation from a high-temperature BCC solid solution to a partially ordered B2 phase and then to a mixed microstructure (disordered BCC plus ordered B2), with the B2 ordering temperature strongly dependent on the Al content and a sharp transformation near 600 °C corresponding to phase separation.
papers.mechanism: Strong composition‐dependent pair interactions (notably between Al and Ni/Co) drive ordering and clustering. The thermodynamic instability (e.g. spinodal behavior) is modulated by temperature and composition, leading to a predictive mapping of phase boundaries under controlled thermal conditions.

papers.title: Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Atomistic molecular dynamics simulations validated against first-principles calculations and limited experimental data to study clustering behavior and ordering under deformation.
papers.findings: Observed that strong clustering exists in the alloy driven by Al–Ni pair correlations (with dominant Al-Al clustering domains), and that increasing temperature reduces but does not eliminate these correlations; under compressive strain, a transition from clustering to ordering occurs.
papers.mechanism: Electronic structure-based linear-response calculations indicate that preferential Al–Ni interactions lead to clustering and predispose the alloy toward ordering transitions. This interaction-driven clustering serves as a thermodynamic precursor to phase transformation, modulated by kinetic effects such as strain.

papers.title: Kinetic ways of tailoring phases in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Experimental investigation of phase selection using various cooling rates during both solidification and solid-state transformation, complemented by CALPHAD calculations to assess phase transformations.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that extremely rapid cooling inhibits the formation of intermetallic phases (σ, γ′, and R phases) while slower cooling allows equilibrium or near-equilibrium phase compositions; the phase selection is directly tied to the kinetics of phase transformation.
papers.mechanism: Sluggish diffusion and kinetic barriers in HEAs play a pivotal role in determining which phases are allowed to form. Even in alloys where thermodynamics would favor multiple phases, the kinetic pathway (cooling rate) can stabilize a metastable single-phase state or lead to a tailored multiphase microstructure.

papers.title: Orientation Relationships in Al0.7CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Microstructural characterization using electron microscopy and energy-dispersive spectroscopy to examine the phase transformation morphology and orientation relationships after quenching.
papers.findings: Identified a Widmanstätten-type microstructure featuring a mixture of a BCC parent phase and an FCC daughter phase, with slight compositional differences (BCC being relatively richer in Al and Cr), highlighting the role of diffusionless and orientation-governed phase transformation mechanisms.
papers.mechanism: The transformation from the high-temperature BCC phase to the FCC phase is controlled by crystallographic orientation relationships that facilitate a diffusionless (martensitic-like) transformation, thereby linking thermal history with phase stability.

established: Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys exhibit phase stability that is strongly dependent on both composition and thermal history.

Thermodynamic instabilities (such as ordering tendencies driven by strong Al-transition metal interactions) are a key factor, as revealed by pair correlation studies and spinodal decomposition analysis.
Kinetic factors, including cooling rate and deformation-induced defect creation, significantly affect phase transformation pathways in high-entropy alloys.

approaches_tried.approach: Monte Carlo simulations with first-principles derived parameters combined with neutron scattering, calorimetry, and in situ microscopy
approaches_tried.outcome: Mapped temperature- and composition-dependent phase transitions (BCC to partially ordered B2 to mixed phases) in Al-containing HEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic molecular dynamics simulations validated against first-principles calculations
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that preferential Al–Ni interactions drive clustering and subsequent ordering, with ordering transitions modulated by strain and temperature.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailoring cooling rates during solidification and solid-state transformations
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that kinetic effects can be exploited to control whether a multiphase equilibrium is reached or a metastable single-phase is retained.

mechanisms: Thermodynamic stabilization via strong Al–transition metal (Ni/Co) pair interactions leading to ordering (e.g., formation of B2 phases) and clustering
Kinetic suppression or enhancement of phase transformations through control of cooling rates, which affects diffusion and nucleation rates
Diffusionless, orientation-dictated transformations (martensitic-like) that arise due to rapid quenching or deformation, linking crystallographic features to phase stability
disagreements: The relative dominance of thermodynamic driving forces versus kinetic barriers; some studies emphasize the predictive power of thermodynamics (e.g., spinodal decomposition and pair interactions) while others highlight the overwhelming influence of kinetic pathways (cooling rates, strain-induced defects).

Variations exist in the predicted temperature ranges for ordering transitions (e.g., B2 ordering) and phase separation boundaries, leading to different interpretations of phase stability under similar processing conditions.
open_questions: How exactly does the balance between composition-dependent thermodynamic instabilities and kinetic factors dictate the stability of the high-temperature BCC phase in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7?
What are the precise temperature and time scales over which the transformation from BCC to ordered (or multiphase) structures occurs in this specific alloy?
Can a singular mechanistic hypothesis fully predict the evolution of phase stability across the entire thermal regime without resorting to empirical adjustments?
opportunities: Perform controlled experiments on Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 that systematically vary thermal history (e.g., isothermal holds versus rapid quenching) to isolate the thermodynamic ordering contributions from kinetic effects.

Integrate atomistic simulations (both MD and Monte Carlo) with CALPHAD predictions to develop a unified model that quantitatively links composition-dependent pair interactions with observed phase transformations.
Establish a baseline by comparing Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 with a similar alloy lacking Cr (or with varied Al content) to directly gauge the influence of specific elemental pairs on phase stability.

Explore the boundary conditions (critical temperatures and cooling rates) that delineate the transition from a high-temperature BCC state to ordered phases, and identify shifts in diffraction patterns or calorimetry signals that could falsify the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.

directions.direction: Investigate the thermodynamic pair interactions, especially the strong Al–Ni/Co correlations that drive spinodal decomposition leading to B2 ordering from the high‐temperature BCC state.
directions.assessment: This direction directly targets the intrinsic thermodynamic instability by relating specific pair interactions to ordering. The evidence from Monte Carlo simulations and pair-probability analyses support such a mechanism (e.g., PMC6207727::web::017::temperature_dependent_ordering_within_th, PMC4976365::web::012::summary). It is well grounded in known physics and feasible with diffraction and calorimetry.

directions.direction: Control the kinetic pathway by varying the cooling rate to modulate the time available for the thermodynamic ordering transformation from BCC to B2.
directions.assessment: This approach decouples kinetic limitations from the thermodynamic driving forces. Prior studies (PMC5043342::web::000::abstract, PMC5043342::web::011::kinetic_effect_and_tailoring_phases_in_c) confirm that cooling rate significantly influences phase selection. This controlled comparison is both informative and experimentally feasible.

directions.direction: Apply a controlled compressive strain during annealing to examine how deformation‐induced defects accelerate or modulate atomic rearrangements leading to ordering.
directions.assessment: Strain has been shown to promote clustering-to-ordering transitions (e.g., PMC4976365::web::007::results_and_discussion). This intervention directly tests the enhancement of ordering kinetics by mechanical activation. The approach is experimentally challenging but offers high informational content regarding defect‐mediated kinetics.

directions.direction: Integrate atomistic simulation (Monte Carlo/DFT) with experimental thermal processing to map out the phase boundaries and quantify the transformation kinetics in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
directions.type: Modelling and simulation combined with characterization
directions.assessment: Simulations that use DFT‐derived pair interaction parameters (PMC6207727::web::006::monte_carlo_model_for_multi_component_tr) offer predictions on ordering temperatures and microstructural evolution that can be validated experimentally. This holistic approach is directly applicable to predicting the mechanism governing phase stability and is well supported by existing evidence.
